newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Labour law cloud's S.Korean Kim's reformist image.
newsitem.headline: Labour law cloud's S.Korean Kim's reformist image.

text.p: South Korea's controversial new labour law has further tarnished President Kim Young-sam's reformist image in an election year, with strikers casting him in the mould of the hated strongmen he replaced.
Kim was South Korea's leading dissident during decades of military rule.
But in the last year he has taken a hawkish stance against rival North Korea, crushed student protests and now ordered the arrest of striking unionists.
"Many South Koreans now openly criticise Kim for his authoritarian style," Shin Jung-hyun, political science professor at Kyunghee University, said on Monday.
"With his reformist image questioned, he has very little to talk about for major achievements."
Shin said with a presidential election scheduled for December, the ruling New Korea Party was cornered after ramming the labour bill through parliament on December 26.
Kim is barred by the constitution from seeking re-election but is expected to seek to anoint a successor.

"If you repeal the (labour) law the credibility of the government will be seriously damaged. If the government presses ahead with its high-handed methods it will face huge resistance locally and internationally," Shin said.

Kim, the first president without a military background for more than three decades, came to power in February 1993 on a reformist ticket and launched a crackdown on corruption and misconduct, legacies from a succession of strongman rulers.
His popularity rating topped 90 percent in his first months in office, when hundreds of senior officials, including members of his own cabinet, were fired for irregularities.
But his popularity has plunged and protesters are now chanting "down with Kim Young-sam" instead of "down with dictators" as they did in demonstrations that Kim spearheaded as an opposition leader.
Seven militant union leaders taking sanctuary in a Seoul cathedral say they aim to topple Kim with a series of strikes that have hobbled South Korea's export-led economy.

And nearly, 2,000 social leaders, including academics, lawyers, and clergy members, have signed a petition calling for the scrapping of the labour law, which allows companies to dismiss workers and replace strikers.
Columnist Chung Koo-jong wrote in the Dong-a Ilbo newspaper that many supporters of the president had left him or planned to do so.
"People are overwhelmed with frustration after witnessing a worse regression in democracy than during the time of authoritarian rule," he wrote.
Chung quoted an unnamed former adviser to Kim as saying: "We have to build democracy from the beginning."
Most South Koreans acknowledge the need for more labour market flexibility, which is provided by the new law.
But they question the decision to extend a ban until 2000 on the militant Korean Confederation of Trade Unions.
Kim's New Korea Party has offered to hold a television debate with union leaders over the new law. But they rejected the offer as a propaganda ploy.
"I think the government pushed through the legislation as it wanted to win conservative votes in the presidential election," said Cho Byung-yong of Korea University's Labour Institute.
Cho said with the economy slowing, the government could win support from businessmen and the middle class for the law.
